query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, increasing the Al/Cr ratio (within a controlled compositional window) promotes the formation of a protective, dual oxide film (α‐Al2O3 and Cr2O3) during high-temperature exposure that in turn helps to stabilize the underlying FCC solid-solution matrix. This stabilization suppresses phase instabilities that would otherwise degrade high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and environmental resistance, while also preserving the FCC deformation mechanisms (e.g., deformation twinning) responsible for cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy processed to yield a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Increase the Al content relative to Cr (i.e. adjust the Al:Cr ratio upward) while keeping the other elemental concentrations constant, contrasted against the baseline equiatomic alloy.
generation.conditions: Process both the modified and baseline alloys identically (using the same melting and casting procedures followed by identical heat treatments) and then expose them to high-temperature oxidation (for high-temperature strength and environmental resistance evaluation) as well as cryogenic mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests at cryogenic temperatures) under otherwise controlled testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, adherent, dual-layer of protective oxides (predominantly α‐Al2O3 and Cr2O3) that maintain the integrity of the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: A higher Al/Cr ratio increases the thermodynamic driving force for forming stable alumina in conjunction with Cr2O3. This oxide scale minimizes further oxidation, limits defect clustering (supporting radiation tolerance), and preserves the dislocation/twinning mechanisms in the FCC matrix, which ensure high cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit improved oxide-scale stability during high-temperature exposure (as measured by a higher fraction of α‐Al2O3 and Cr2O3), better retention of high-temperature mechanical properties and radiation resistance, and maintained or slightly enhanced cryogenic toughness via sustained deformation twinning. The magnitude of these improvements is uncertain outside the identified compositional window.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a balanced Al and Cr content.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within a compositional range that avoids the formation of brittle BCC phases or undesirable intermetallic precipitates; it is specifically valid for alloys processed to form a single-phase FCC structure and for conditions where the controlled oxidation kinetics allow protective oxide layer formation.
generation.uncertainty: While the link between the Al/Cr ratio and oxide-scale formation is supported by oxidation modeling studies, the quantitative impact on radiation tolerance and cryogenic toughness remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys: one baseline equiatomic and one with an increased Al/Cr ratio (keeping all other elements equal). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation tests (evaluating oxide scale formation via SEM/EDS and XRD) as well as mechanical testing at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., tensile tests capturing yield strength and ductility).
measurements: Quantitative phase analysis of the oxide scale (proportion of α‐Al2O3 and Cr2O3) after high-temperature exposure
High-temperature mechanical property retention (e.g., hardness, tensile strength)
Cryogenic tensile ductility and evidence of deformation twinning (using microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with the higher Al/Cr ratio does not form a significantly more protective dual oxide layer, or if it fails to show improved high-temperature stability, radiation tolerance indicators, or cryogenic toughness (compared to the baseline), then the hypothesis that the Al/Cr ratio governs phase stability via protective oxide formation is falsified.
